title: Succession Drama: Who Gets the Crown?
paragraphs: King David was getting super old. The years had really caught up with him. Even with a ton of blankets, he was always cold. So his crew was like, "Yo, we should find a young virgin to hang out with the king and take care of him. She can get in bed with you and, you know, warm you up."

So they scouted the whole country of Israel for the most beautiful girl they could find. They found this girl Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king. She was seriously stunning. She stayed by his side and took care of him, but the king never hooked up with her.

Meanwhile, Adonijah, whose mom was Haggith, got all cocky and was like, "I'm the next king!" He made a huge deal out of it, with chariots and horsemen and fifty dudes running ahead of him. His dad had always let him do whatever he wanted and never told him off, not even once. Plus, he was a really good-looking guy and was next in line after Absalom.

Adonijah teamed up with Joab, son of Zeruiah, and Abiathar the priest, and they totally backed his play. But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei and Rei, and David's own bodyguards were not on board with Adonijah.

Next thing you know, Adonijah threw a big coronation party, sacrificing a bunch of sheep, cattle, and prime beef at the Stone of Zoheleth near the Rogel Spring. He invited all his brothers—the king's sons—and all the important people in Judah. But he totally snubbed Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the bodyguards, and his own brother Solomon.

Nathan went straight to Bathsheba, Solomon's mom, and said, "Have you heard? Adonijah, Haggith's son, has made himself king, and our master David has no idea. Quick, listen up. I'll tell you how to save your own life and Solomon's. Go to King David right now and be like, 'My king, didn't you promise me that my son Solomon would be king after you and sit on your throne? So why is Adonijah king now?' While you're talking to him, I'll come in and back you up."
Bathsheba went to the king's bedroom right away. He was so, so old. Abishag was there, making sure he was comfortable. Bathsheba bowed down to show respect, and the king asked, "What do you need?"

She said, "My master, you promised me in God's name, 'Your son Solomon will be king after me and sit on my throne.' But now, look, Adonijah has made himself king, and you don't even know! He's thrown this massive coronation party with tons of food, inviting all the king's sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab, the head of the army. But he didn't invite your servant Solomon. My king, the whole country is watching you to see what you'll do, to see who will take the throne after you. If you don't do something, the second you're gone, my son Solomon and I are basically dead meat."
Just then, while she was still talking, Nathan the prophet showed up. They announced, "Nathan the prophet is here." He came in and bowed low before the king, with his face to the ground.

Nathan started, "My king, did you actually say, 'Adonijah will be king after me and sit on my throne'? Because that's what's happening right now. He's throwing a huge party, inviting all the king's sons, the army officers, and Abiathar the priest. They're all eating and drinking and shouting, 'Long live King Adonijah!' But I wasn't invited, and neither was Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, or your servant Solomon. Did you do this behind our backs? Did you not tell us who you wanted to be king after you?"
King David finally took action. "Get Bathsheba back in here." She came and stood before him.

The king made a solemn promise, "As surely as God lives, the God who has saved me from all my troubles, I will do exactly what I promised in the name of the God of Israel: Your son Solomon will be king after me and will take my place on the throne. And I'm making it happen today."
Bathsheba bowed down again, her face to the ground. She knelt before the king and said, "May my master, King David, live forever!"
King David then commanded, "Call Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada." They all came to the king.

He ordered them, "Get my servants, put my son Solomon on my own royal mule, and lead him down to Gihon. When you get there, Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet will anoint him king over Israel. Then, blow the ram's horn and shout, 'Long live King Solomon!' You will then come back with him, and he will sit on my throne as the new king. I have officially named him ruler over Israel and Judah."

Benaiah son of Jehoiada replied, "Yes! And may the LORD, the God of my master the king, make it so! Just as God has been with you, may he be with Solomon and make his kingdom even greater than yours!"

So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the king's personal bodyguards (the Kerethites and Pelethites) went down, put Solomon on King David's mule, and led him in a parade to Gihon. Zadok the priest brought a flask of oil from the holy tent and anointed Solomon. They blew the ram's horn, and everyone shouted, "Long live King Solomon!" The whole crowd joined in, with music playing and people singing so loud that the ground was shaking.

Adonijah and his guests were just finishing up their own 'coronation' feast when they heard all the noise. When Joab heard the ram's horn, he was like, "What is all that noise? What's going on in the city?"
Just as he said that, Jonathan, son of Abiathar the priest, showed up. Adonijah said, "Come in! A good man like you must have good news."

But Jonathan said, "Not really. Our master King David has just made Solomon king! The king sent Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Kerethites and Pelethites with him. They put Solomon on the king's own mule. Then Zadok and Nathan anointed him king at Gihon, and now they're all parading back, celebrating like crazy. The whole city is in an uproar! That's the noise you're hearing. And get this—Solomon is now sitting on the royal throne! What's more, the king's own officials have come to congratulate King David, saying, 'May your God make Solomon's name even more famous than yours and his kingdom greater than yours!' And the king, on his deathbed, bowed in worship and prayed, 'Praise be to the LORD, the God of Israel, who has given me a successor to my throne, and I have lived to see it!'"

At this point, Adonijah's guests all panicked and scattered in every direction. But Adonijah himself was terrified of Solomon. He ran to the sanctuary and grabbed onto the horns of the altar for safety.
Someone told Solomon, "Adonijah is scared of you, King Solomon. He's holding onto the horns of the altar and saying, 'I won't leave until King Solomon promises not to kill me.'"

Solomon replied, "If he acts like an honorable man, not a single hair on his head will be touched. But if he's up to no good, he will die." Then King Solomon sent for him, and they brought him from the altar. Adonijah came and bowed down to King Solomon. Solomon just told him, "Go home."

title: David's Last Words & Solomon's Power Moves
paragraphs: When it was almost time for David to die, he gave his son Solomon these final instructions: “Look, I’m about to go the way everyone on earth does. But you—you gotta be strong and show them what you’re made of. Do what God tells you to. Follow the path he lays out for you, stick to his life-map, and watch for the signs he gives. It’s all in the rules he gave to Moses. If you do that, you’ll succeed in whatever you do, wherever you go. Then God will keep the promise he made to me, saying, ‘If your sons watch their steps and stay true to me with all their heart and soul, you’ll always have someone on Israel’s throne.’

“And listen, don’t forget what Joab, son of Zeruiah, did to the two commanders of Israel’s army, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. He straight-up murdered them in cold blood during peacetime, like it was war. He’s been stained with that blood ever since. You know what’s best, but whatever you do, don’t let him get away with it. Make him pay.
“But be good to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite. Show them hospitality, because that’s how they treated me when I was on the run from your brother Absalom.

“You also have to deal with Shimei son of Gera the Benjaminite from Bahurim. He’s the one who cursed me out so bad when I was heading to Mahanaim. But later, when he met me at the Jordan River, I swore to him by God that I wouldn’t kill him. Still, you can’t just let him off the hook. You’re a smart guy; you’ll know what to do to make sure he pays before he dies.”

Then David passed away and was buried in the City of David. He had ruled Israel for forty years—seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. Solomon then took over his father David’s throne and had a solid grip on the kingdom.
One day, Adonijah, son of Haggith, went to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mom. She asked him, “Are you here in peace?”
He said, “Yeah, in peace.” Then he added, “Can I ask you something?”
“Go ahead,” she said.

“You know,” he started, “the kingdom was basically mine. Everyone expected me to be the next king. But then the whole thing flipped, and my brother got the crown instead—it was God’s plan. So now I just have one small favor to ask. Please don’t say no.”
“Okay, ask,” she said.
“Could you ask King Solomon to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife? He won’t say no to you.”
“Sure,” Bathsheba said. “I’ll talk to the king for you.”

So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to ask on Adonijah’s behalf. The king stood up to welcome her, bowed respectfully, and sat back on his throne. He even had a throne brought for his mother, and she sat at his right side.
She said, “I have a small favor to ask. Please don’t refuse me.”
The king replied, “Go ahead, Mom. Of course I won’t refuse you.”
She said, “Please give Abishag the Shunammite to your brother Adonijah as his wife.”

King Solomon shot back at his mother, “What kind of favor is that, asking that Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah? Why don’t you just ask me to hand over the entire kingdom to him? He’s my older brother, and he has Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah on his side!”

Then King Solomon swore to God, “May God strike me down if Adonijah doesn’t pay for this with his life! As surely as God lives—the one who put me on my father David’s throne and gave me this kingdom just as he promised—Adonijah will die for this. Today!”
So King Solomon sent Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, who struck Adonijah down, and he died.

Then the king told Abiathar the priest, “You’re exiled to your land in Anathoth. You deserve to die, but I’m not going to kill you, at least not right now. You carried the Ark of the Lord GOD with my father David and went through all the hard times with him.”
Solomon then fired Abiathar from his job as a priest, which fulfilled what God had said at Shiloh about Eli’s family.

When Joab heard the news—and remember, this is the same Joab who had sided with Adonijah but not with Absalom—he ran to God’s sanctuary and grabbed onto the horns of the altar, holding on for dear life. Someone told King Solomon that Joab had fled to the sanctuary and was clinging to the altar. Solomon immediately sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada with the order: “Go kill him.”
Benaiah went to the sanctuary of God and said, “The king’s orders: come out.”
Joab replied, “No, I’ll die right here.”
Benaiah went back and told the king what Joab had said.

The king responded, “Fine, do what he says. Kill him and bury him. This will clear me and my father’s family of the guilt from Joab’s senseless murders. God is making Joab pay for those murders. He killed two men who were way better than him: Abner son of Ner, the commander of Israel's army, and Amasa son of Jether, the commander of Judah's army. He did it behind my father’s back. The responsibility for their deaths is on Joab and his family forever. But for David, his descendants, and his kingdom, there will be peace from God.”

So Benaiah son of Jehoiada went back, struck Joab, and killed him. He was buried at his home in the desert. The king then made Benaiah son of Jehoiada the new army commander instead of Joab, and he replaced Abiathar with Zadok the priest.

Next, the king summoned Shimei and told him, “Build a house for yourself in Jerusalem and live there. But you are not to leave the city. The moment you cross the Kidron Brook, you’re a dead man—and it’ll be your own fault.”
Shimei replied, “Sounds good, my lord and king. I’ll do exactly what you say.” And Shimei lived in Jerusalem for a long time.

But about three years later, two of Shimei’s slaves ran away to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath. Someone told Shimei, “Hey, your slaves are in Gath.” So Shimei got up, saddled his donkey, and went to Gath to find his slaves. He found them and brought them back.
When Solomon heard that Shimei had left Jerusalem for Gath and returned, he called for him.

Solomon said to Shimei, "Didn't I make you swear to God and warn you that if you ever left this area, you’d be signing your own death warrant? And didn’t you say, ‘Sounds good, I’ll do exactly what you say’? So why didn’t you keep your promise to God and follow my orders?”

Then the king said to Shimei, “You know deep down all the messed-up things you did to my father David. Now God is making you pay for that evil. But King Solomon will be blessed, and David’s throne will be secure before God forever.”
Then the king gave the order to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who went out and struck Shimei down, and he died.
And just like that, the kingdom was firmly in Solomon’s control.

title: Solomon Asks For Wisdom, Gets a WILD First Test
paragraphs: So, Solomon made a political move and married the daughter of Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. He brought her to Jerusalem, the City of David, to stay while he was finishing up his huge building projects: his own palace, God's Temple, and the wall around the city. At this point, people were just worshiping wherever, at these local shrines, because the official Temple for God hadn't been built yet. Solomon genuinely loved God and mostly followed the good example his dad David set, but he did also use those local shrines for sacrifices and stuff.

The king traveled to Gibeon, which was like the most popular shrine, to worship. He went all out and offered a thousand sacrifices on the altar there. And that night, in Gibeon, God showed up in Solomon's dream and said, "What do you want? Ask for anything."

Solomon answered, "You were incredibly good and loving to my father David because he was faithful to you, lived right, and had a pure heart. And you've kept up that amazing love by letting his own son—me!—take his throne today.

"And now, here I am. My God, you made me the king instead of my dad, David. But I'm super young and feel like I have no idea what I'm doing. I'm just a kid, really. I don't know the first thing about leading. And I'm in charge of your chosen people, a nation so huge you can't even count them all.

"So this is what I want: Give me a heart that listens to you so I can lead your people well and tell the difference between right and wrong. Because, for real, who could possibly lead this amazing nation of yours on their own?"

God was seriously pleased with Solomon's answer. He said to him, "Because you asked for this—and you didn't ask for a long life, or to be rich, or for your enemies to be defeated, but you asked for the wisdom to be a good and fair leader—I'm giving you exactly what you asked for. I'm giving you a heart full of wisdom and understanding. There has never been anyone like you before, and there never will be again. And on top of that, I'm giving you the wealth and fame you *didn't* ask for. No other king will even come close to you. And if you stick with me and follow my rules, just like your dad David did, I'll give you a long life too."

Solomon woke up and was like, whoa, what a dream! He went back to Jerusalem, stood before the Ark of the Covenant, and worshiped God with more sacrifices and offerings. Then he threw a massive party for all his officials.

Literally the next thing that happened, two prostitutes came to the king for his judgment. The first woman said, "Sir, this woman and I live in the same house. I had a baby while we were living there. Three days later, she had a baby too. It was just the two of us in the house, nobody else. One night, this woman's baby died because she rolled over on him in her sleep. So she got up in the middle of the night, took my son from my side while I was totally asleep, put him in her bed, and put her dead baby in my bed. When I woke up in the morning to feed my son, I found a dead baby! But when I looked closer in the daylight, I knew right away it wasn't my son."
"That's a lie!" the other woman shouted. "The living baby is mine, and the dead one is yours!"
The first woman shot back, "No! Your son is the dead one, and mine is the living one!"
They kept arguing like this right in front of the king.
The king thought for a second and said, "Okay, so this woman says, 'The living baby is mine, the dead one is yours,' and the other one says, 'No, the dead one is yours, and the living one is mine.'"
After a moment, the king said, "Bring me a sword." So they brought him a sword.
Then he gave the order: "Cut the living baby in two. Give half to one woman and half to the other."
The real mother of the living baby, filled with love for her son, cried out, "Oh no, my lord! Please, give her the baby, just don't kill him!"
But the other woman said, "Fine by me. If I can't have him, neither can you. Go ahead, cut him!"
The king made his decision: "Give the living baby to the first woman. Do not kill him. She is the real mother."
News of the king's ruling spread like wildfire through Israel. Everyone was in awe of him, realizing he had wisdom from God that allowed him to make such a just decision.

title: Solomon's Kingdom Was Lowkey Stacked
paragraphs: So, King Solomon was off to a great start, ruling over all of Israel.
Here's the rundown of his top officials:

Azariah son of Zadok was the main priest. Elihoreph and Ahijah, who were Shisha's sons, were the secretaries. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the historian, keeping track of everything. Benaiah son of Jehoiada was the commander of the army. Zadok and Abiathar were also priests. Azariah son of Nathan was in charge of all the regional managers. Zabud son of Nathan was a priest and one of the king's close friends. Ahishar was the manager of the palace, and Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of all the labor projects.

Solomon had twelve regional managers spread out across Israel. They were responsible for getting supplies for the king and his entire administration. Each one handled the supplies for one month out of the year. Here are their names:
Ben-Hur was in the hills of Ephraim.
Ben-Deker was in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth Shemesh, and Elon Bethhanan.
Ben-Hesed was in Arubboth, which also covered Socoh and all of Hepher.
Ben-Abinadab was in Naphoth Dor (fun fact, he was married to Solomon's daughter, Taphath).
Baana son of Ahilud was in Taanach and Megiddo, and all of Beth Shan near Zarethan, below Jezreel, and from Beth Shan to Abel Meholah, all the way to Jokmeam.
Ben-Geber was in Ramoth Gilead. His area included the villages of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead and the Argob region in Bashan, which had sixty huge walled cities with gates reinforced with bronze.
Ahinadab son of Iddo was in Mahanaim.
Ahimaaz was in Naphtali (he also married one of Solomon's daughters, Basemath).
Baana son of Hushai was in Asher and Aloth.
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah was in Issachar.
Shimei son of Ela was in Benjamin.
Geber son of Uri was in Gilead, which was the land of King Sihon of the Amorites and King Og of Bashan. This dude managed that whole district all by himself.

Judah and Israel had a crazy number of people—like the sand on a beach! They had everything they needed, just eating, drinking, and living happy lives. Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates River in the east all the way to the land of the Philistines in the west, right up to the border of Egypt. All these places paid him tribute and were under his rule for his entire life.
To give you an idea, the food supply for Solomon's household for just one day was:
185 bushels of fine flour
375 bushels of regular meal
10 cattle that were grain-fed
20 cattle from the pasture
100 sheep
and a random mix of deer, gazelles, roebucks, and some fancy birds.

Solomon was the ruler of everything and everyone west of the Euphrates River, from Tiphsah to Gaza. There was peace everywhere. For Solomon's entire life, everyone in Israel and Judah, from Dan in the north all the way to Beersheba in the south, lived in safety and were totally content with what they had.

Solomon had 40,000 stalls for his chariot horses and 12,000 horsemen. The regional managers, each in their assigned month, made sure there were enough food supplies for King Solomon and everyone who ate at his table. They never ran out of anything. They also had to bring their quota of barley and straw for the horses to the right place.

God gave Solomon some next-level wisdom—like, the deepest understanding and a huge heart. There was nothing he couldn't figure out, no problem he couldn't handle. Solomon's wisdom was way beyond the famous wisdom of the wise men from the East and even outshone the legendary wisdom of Egypt. He was literally wiser than anyone—wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, wiser than Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. He got famous in all the surrounding nations. He came up with 3,000 proverbs and wrote 1,005 songs. He was basically a walking encyclopedia on plants, from the giant cedars of Lebanon to the tiny hyssop that grows in wall cracks. He knew everything about animals, birds, reptiles, and fish. Kings from all over the world heard about how wise he was and sent people, so folks came from everywhere just to listen to Solomon's wisdom.

title: Solomon's Epic Temple Build ft. King Hiram
paragraphs: So, King Hiram of Tyre, who had been close friends with King David his whole life, sent his people to congratulate Solomon on becoming king. Solomon sent him a message back, saying, "You know my dad David couldn’t build a temple for God because he was constantly dealing with wars on all sides, until God finally shut them down. But now, God has blessed us with peace all around—no enemies, no drama.

“So here’s the deal: I’m going to build a temple for my God, just like God promised my dad, David. He was like, ‘Your son, the one I’ll set up to be king after you, he’s the one who will build a house in my name.’ And this is where you come in: Can you order your guys to cut down some cedars from the Lebanon forest? My loggers will work with your crew, and I’ll pay your guys whatever you say is fair. We both know that there is no one like you Sidonians for cutting timber.”
When Hiram got Solomon’s message, he was delighted. He said, "Blessed be God for giving David such a wise son to rule this amazing nation!”

Then he sent this message to Solomon: "I got your request for the cedars and cypresses. It's as good as done—your wish is my command. My lumberjacks will haul the timbers from Lebanon to the sea, build them into rafts, and float them to the spot you pick. Then they’ll take them apart for you to haul away. All I need from you is to feed my crew.”

So Hiram supplied all the cedar and cypress wood that Solomon wanted. In return, Solomon gave Hiram 125,000 bushels of wheat and 115,000 gallons of top-shelf olive oil. He did this every single year. And God, for his part, gave Solomon wisdom, just like he promised. The solid peace between Hiram and Solomon was made official with a treaty.

King Solomon put together a massive crew of thirty thousand men from all over Israel. He sent them to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand a month; they’d work a month in Lebanon and then get two months off at home. Adoniram was the manager of the whole operation. Solomon also had seventy thousand regular laborers and another eighty thousand stonecutters up in the hills—plus thirty-three hundred foremen who managed the project and supervised the work crews. Following the king’s orders, they dug up these huge, high-quality blocks of stone—perfectly cut for the foundation of The Temple. Solomon and Hiram’s construction workers, with some help from the guys from Gebal, cut and prepared all the timber and stone for building The Temple.

title: Solomon's GOATED Temple Build!
paragraphs: Okay, so get this: 480 years after the Israelites left Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's rule, in the month of Ziv (the second month), King Solomon started building the Temple of God. This thing was huge—like, 90 feet long, 30 feet wide, and 45 feet high. It had this cool 30-foot-wide porch stretching across the front, going out 15 feet. Inside, the windows were these narrow, deep-set things. And on the outside, he built this whole support structure with extra rooms. The first floor rooms were 7.5 feet wide, the second 9 feet, and the third 10.5 feet. He even built these ledges on the outside to hold up the support beams. Pretty smart, right?

And here's the wild part: all the stones were cut and prepped at the quarry. That means the actual construction site was super quiet and respectful—no loud banging from hammers or anything. That's some next-level planning.

The main entrance was on the south side, with stairs going up to the second floor, then to the third. Solomon saw the whole project through, finishing it with a roof of cedar beams and planks. That support structure on the outside? It was connected to the temple with more cedar beams, and the rooms inside were seven and a half feet high.

Then God gave Solomon a message: 'About this temple you're building... what really matters is that you live by my rules and actually do what I say. If you follow my instructions, I'll make good on the promise I gave your dad, David. I'll literally come and live with the Israelites. I'm not gonna abandon my people.'

So Solomon finished building the Temple. He covered the inside walls from top to bottom with cedar planks, and used cypress for the floors. He sectioned off the back 30 feet to be the Inner Sanctuary, the Holy of Holies, with cedar from floor to ceiling. The main room in front of it was 60 feet long. The whole inside was cedar, carved with fruits and flowers. All cedar, so you couldn't see any of the stone.

The Inner Sanctuary was made to hold the Ark of the Covenant of God. It was a perfect cube, 30 feet on each side, and completely covered in gold. The cedar altar was also covered in gold. It was pure gold everywhere you looked—gold chains in front of the gold-plated Inner Sanctuary... just gold everywhere. Walls, ceiling, floor, altar. It was dazzling!

Then he made two giant angel-like figures called cherubim out of olivewood. Each one was 15 feet tall. Their wings were also 15 feet across, and they were identical. He put them in the Inner Sanctuary with their wings spread out. Their wings stretched across the whole room—one wing touched one wall, the other wing touched the other wall, and their wings met in the middle. And yeah, the cherubim were covered in gold too.
He then had carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and flowers put on all the walls of both the Inner and Main Sanctuaries. And all the floors in both rooms were plated with gold.
He made olivewood doors for the entrance to the Inner Sanctuary, with a five-sided frame. The doors were also carved with cherubim, palm trees, and flowers, and then covered in gold.

He did something similar for the entrance to the Main Sanctuary, using olivewood for the doorposts, but these were four-sided. The doors were made of cypress and split into two panels that could swing separately. These were also carved with cherubim, palm trees, and flowers, and covered with hammered gold.
He built the inner court with three layers of cut stones and a layer of cedar timbers on top.

The foundation for God's Temple was laid in the fourth year of Solomon's reign, in the month of Ziv. It was completely finished in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul (the eighth month), exactly as planned. It took Solomon seven years to build it.

title: Solomon's Palace & Temple Bling: The Ultimate Flex
paragraphs: It took Solomon another thirteen years to finish building his own palace complex. He built the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon, which was a massive 150 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high. It had four rows of cedar columns holding up 45 cedar beams, with 15 in each row, and a cedar roof. There were windows in groups of three on both sides, set high up. All the doors were rectangular and perfectly symmetrical.
He also built a courtyard with columns that was 75 feet long and 45 feet wide. It had a covered porch at the front with some serious eaves.
Then he built a courtroom, the Hall of Justice, where he'd make his big decisions. It was all paneled with cedar, super fancy.
His own house was built behind the Hall with a similar design. Solomon also built another one just like it for Pharaoh’s daughter, who he was married to.

They didn't cheap out on anything. Everything, inside and out, from the foundation to the roof, was made with top-quality stone that was cut, shaped, and polished perfectly. The foundation stones were huge, like 12 to 15 feet long, and the best you could get. They used the finest stone on top of the foundation, all shaped to size and trimmed with cedar. The courtyard was walled off with three layers of stone and topped with cedar timbers, just like the porch of God's Temple.

King Solomon sent for a guy named Hiram from Tyre (not the king, a different Hiram). Hiram's mom was a widow from the Naphtali tribe, and his dad was a Tyrian and a master at working with bronze. This Hiram guy was a true artist—he could make anything out of bronze. So he came to King Solomon and did all the bronze work for him.

First, he made two huge bronze pillars, each 27 feet tall and 18 feet around. Then he made two bronze capitals to go on top of the pillars. Each capital was 7.5 feet high and flared out at the top like a lily. Each one was decorated with a fancy design of seven braided chains and two rows of 200 pomegranates, which made the pillars look amazing. He set up the pillars at the entrance to the Temple. The one on the south he named Jachin (which means 'Security') and the one on the north he named Boaz (which means 'Stability'). The capitals were shaped like lilies.

After the pillars were done, Hiram's next big project was the Sea—a giant round basin made of cast metal. It was 15 feet across, 7.5 feet tall, and 45 feet around. Right under the rim, there were two rows of decorative gourds, ten gourds for every foot and a half. The gourds were all one piece with the Sea.

The Sea was set on twelve bronze bulls. Three faced north, three faced west, three faced south, and three faced east. The bulls were facing outward, holding up the Sea on their backs. The Sea itself was three inches thick and its rim flared out like a cup or a lily. It could hold about 11,500 gallons of water, which is wild.

Hiram also made ten bronze washstands. Each one was six feet square and 4.5 feet tall. They were built with panels attached to uprights. The panels and uprights had lions, bulls, and cherubim on them. There was beveled wreath-work bordering the lions and bulls above and below. Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles. The uprights had decorative relief work cast into them. Each stand held a basin on a circular, engraved support that was a foot and a half deep, set on a pedestal that was two and a quarter feet square. The washstand itself was square. The axles were attached under the stand, and the wheels were fixed to them. The wheels were 27 inches in diameter and looked like chariot wheels. Everything—axles, rims, spokes, and hubs—was made of cast metal.

There was a handle at each of the four corners of the washstands, and the handles were cast as one piece with the stand. At the top of the washstand, there was a ring about nine inches deep. The uprights and handles were all cast with the stand. Every available surface was engraved with cherubim, lions, and palm trees, bordered by cool patterns. All the washstands were identical, made from the same mold.

He also made ten bronze washbasins, each six feet across and able to hold 230 gallons. There was one basin for each of the ten washstands. He put five stands on the south side of the Temple and five on the north. The Sea was placed at the southeast corner of the Temple. Then Hiram made all the other tools: buckets, shovels, and bowls.
Hiram finished all the work he was supposed to do for King Solomon on God's Temple:

two pillars; two capitals on top of the pillars; two decorative filigrees for the capitals; four hundred pomegranates for the two filigrees (a double row for each); ten washstands, each with its own washbasin; one Sea; twelve bulls under the Sea; and all the buckets, shovels, and bowls.

All these things that Hiram made for King Solomon for God's Temple were made of polished bronze. He cast them in clay molds in a foundry on the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarethan. There were so many of these items that they never even weighed them. Nobody knows how much bronze was actually used.
Solomon was also in charge of all the furniture and accessories in God's Temple:

the gold Altar; the gold Table that held the Bread of the Presence; the pure gold candelabras, five on the right and five on the left in front of the Inner Sanctuary; the gold flowers, lamps, and tongs; the pure gold dishes, wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, ladles, and censers; and the gold sockets for the doors of the Inner Sanctuary, the Holy of Holies, which were also used for the doors of the Main Sanctuary.

And that was it. All the work King Solomon did on God's Temple was finished. Then he brought in all the stuff his father David had dedicated—the silver, the gold, and all the artifacts. He put everything in the treasury of God's Temple.

title: Solomon's Epic Temple Dedication & Prayer
paragraphs: Alright, so to get this massive project to the finish line, King Solomon called in all the honored ones of Israel—we're talking all the tribe leaders and the heads of the big families. The goal was to bring up the Ark of God's Covenant from Zion, the City of David. And dude, everyone came. All of Israel was there with King Solomon in the seventh month, Ethanim, for the huge autumn festival.

With all of Israel's leaders there, the priests picked up the Ark of God. They carried the Ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the holy gear that went with it. King Solomon and the entire crowd of Israel were right there at the Ark, worshiping and sacrificing a wild number of sheep and cattle—so many that nobody could even keep count.

Then the priests brought the Ark of God's Covenant to its designated spot in the Inner Sanctuary, the Most Holy Place, right under the wings of the cherubim. The cherubim's wings were spread out over the Ark and its carrying poles. The poles were so long you could see the ends from the entrance of the Inner Sanctuary, but you couldn't see them from any farther out. They're actually still there today. There was nothing inside the Ark except for the two stone tablets that Moses put in it back at Horeb, where God made a covenant with Israel after He brought them out of Egypt.

When the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud just filled The Temple of God. It was so thick the priests couldn't even do their duties because of it—the glory of God had totally filled the Temple!
Then Solomon spoke up:
"God told us He lives in a thick darkness where no one can see Him; but I've built this amazing Temple for you, O God, to be your home forever."
The king then turned to the whole crowd and blessed them:

"Shoutout to God, the God of Israel, who personally spoke to my dad, David. And now He's kept the promise He made when He said, 'Ever since I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I haven't chosen one city from all the tribes of Israel to build a Temple for my Name. But I did choose David to lead my people Israel.'

"My dad, David, really wanted to build a Temple to honor the Name of God, the God of Israel. But God told him, 'It's awesome that you wanted to build a Temple in my honor—major props! But you're not the one who's gonna build it. Your son will build it to honor my Name.'

"God did exactly what He said He would. I've taken over from my dad David and now I rule Israel, just like God promised. And now I've built this Temple to honor God, the God of Israel. I've also made a place for the Ark that holds the covenant of God, the one He made with our ancestors when He brought them out of Egypt."
In front of the whole crowd of Israel, Solomon stood before the Altar, spread his hands out to the sky, and prayed,

"O God, God of Israel, there is no god like you in heaven above or on earth below. You're the one who always keeps your promises and relentlessly loves your servants when they're sincerely trying to live your way. You kept your word to my dad David, your personal promise. You did exactly what you said you would—every single detail. The proof is right here, today!

"So keep it up, God, O God of Israel! Keep the promises you made to my dad David when you said, 'You'll always have a descendant to rule on Israel's throne, as long as your sons are careful to live in my presence just like you have.'
"O God of Israel, please make it all happen; confirm it and lock it in!

"But for real, is God actually going to move into our neighborhood? I mean, the whole universe isn't big enough for you, let alone this Temple I've built. But still, I'm bold enough to ask: please pay attention to my prayers, the ones for everyone and the ones just for me, O God, my God. Listen to my passionate prayers that I'm laying out before you right now. Keep your eyes on this Temple day and night, this place you said 'My Name will be there,' and listen to the prayers I pray here.
"Listen from your home in heaven, and when you hear, please forgive.

"When someone wrongs a neighbor and promises to make it right, and then comes and says the same promise before your Altar in this Temple, listen from heaven and do something about it. Judge your people, make the guilty person pay for what they did, and let the innocent person go free.
"When your people Israel get defeated by an enemy because they've sinned against you, but then they turn back to you, acknowledge your name, and pray their hearts out in this Temple,
"Listen from your home in heaven, forgive the sin of your people Israel, and bring them back to the land you gave their ancestors.
"When the sky dries up and there's no rain because your people have sinned against you, but then they pray toward this place, acknowledge your name, and stop sinning because you've disciplined them,
"Listen from your home in heaven, and forgive the sins of your servants, your people Israel.
"Then start over with them: teach them how to live right, and send rain on the land you gave your people as their own.

"When disasters hit—famine, disease, crop failure, plagues of locusts or beetles, or when an enemy army surrounds their cities—whatever the disaster, whatever the prayer from anyone in your people Israel, when their hearts are broken by the disaster and they throw their hands up to this Temple for help,
"Listen from your home in heaven.

"Forgive them and get to work on us. Give each person what they deserve, because you know what's in their hearts (you're the only one who truly knows people from the inside out!). That way, they'll always respect and trust you on this land you gave our ancestors.

"And don't forget the foreigner who isn't one of your people Israel but has come from a faraway country because they heard about you. People are going to hear about your great name and your amazing power, and they'll come to pray at this Temple.
"Listen from your home in heaven.

"Answer the foreigner's prayers so that people all over the world will know who you are and will respect you, just like your own people Israel do. Then they'll know that you have personally made this Temple that I've built special.
"When your people go to war against their enemies wherever you send them, and they pray to you facing this city you chose and this Temple I've built for your Name,
"Listen from heaven to their prayer and their request, and fight for them.

"When they sin against you—and let's be real, they will; no one is perfect—and in your anger you let their enemies capture them and take them to another country, far or near, but then they have a change of heart in that country and they repent and pray, 'We've sinned, we've done wrong, we've been so wicked,' and they turn back to you with all their heart and soul in the land of their enemies, and they pray to you facing their homeland, the land you gave their ancestors, toward the city you chose, and this Temple I built for your Name,
"Listen from your home in heaven to their desperate prayers and do what's best for them.

"Forgive your people who have sinned against you; forgive all their rebellions and make their captors be merciful to them. Because they are your people, your precious inheritance that you rescued from the fiery furnace of Egypt!

"So please be alert and listen to the prayers of me, your servant, and your people Israel; listen every time they cry out to you! You chose them from all the peoples on earth to be your very own, just as you announced through your servant Moses when you, O God, our powerful ruler, brought our ancestors out of Egypt."

After Solomon finished praying all these bold and passionate prayers to God, he stood up from before God's Altar, where he had been kneeling with his hands stretched up to heaven. Standing up, he blessed the whole crowd of Israel, shouting at the top of his lungs:

"Praise God, who has given rest to his people Israel, just like he promised. Not a single one of the good promises he made through Moses has failed. May God, our God, stay with us just like he was with our ancestors—may he never leave us or give up on us. May he keep our hearts focused on him, so we follow the path he has laid out, keeping the commands, rules, and laws he gave our ancestors.

"And may these words I've prayed to God be always on his mind, day and night, so he'll do what's right for me and for his people Israel, day after day. Then all the people on earth will know that the LORD is God; there is no other. And you guys, you have to be completely devoted to God, our God, following his ways and paying attention to everything he has made clear today."

Then the king and all Israel with him worshiped, offering sacrifices to God. Solomon offered Peace-Offerings, sacrificing 22,000 cattle and 120,000 sheep to God. That's how the king and all of Israel dedicated The Temple of God.

On that same day, the king consecrated the central area of the courtyard in front of God's Temple. He sacrificed the Burnt-Offerings, Grain-Offerings, and the fat from the Peace-Offerings there because the bronze Altar was too small to handle everything.

So Solomon and all Israel celebrated the great autumn festival—a massive crowd of people from as far as the Entrance of Hamath in the northeast to the Brook of Egypt in the southwest. They celebrated for seven days, and then they did it all over again for another seven days! Two whole weeks of partying! Then he sent them home. They blessed the king and went home, super happy and grateful for all the good things God had done for his servant David and for his people Israel.

title: Solomon's Big Flex & God's Ultimatum
paragraphs: So after Solomon finished building God's Temple and his own epic palace—all the huge projects he'd been dreaming of—God appeared to him again, just like that time in Gibeon.

And God told him, "I've heard all your prayers, your super passionate ones. I've made this Temple you built sacred. My Name is on it forever; I'll always be watching over it and my heart is in it. As for you, if you live your life for me like your dad David did, with a pure heart and good actions, following the life I've laid out for you and obeying my rules, then I'll make sure your kingdom over Israel is secure, built on a solid foundation. The same promise I gave your dad David, I'm giving you: 'You'll always have a descendant on Israel's throne.'

"But if you or your sons turn your back on me, ignore my guidance, and start following other gods by serving and worshipping them, then the deal is off. I'll wipe Israel right off the map and reject this Temple I've just made sacred for my Name. Israel will become a total joke to the world. And this Temple, as amazing as it is now, will be looked down on. People will see the ruins and ask, 'What on earth happened here?' And they'll be told, 'The people who lived here betrayed their God, the same God who rescued their ancestors from Egypt. They started following other gods, worshipping and serving them. That's why God brought all this destruction on them.'"

After 20 years of building the two main structures, God's Temple and his own palace, Solomon gave Hiram, the king of Tyre, a gift of twenty towns in Galilee. Hiram had supplied him with all the cedar, cypress, and gold he wanted. But when Hiram came from Tyre to check out the towns Solomon had given him, he was not impressed.
He said, "What kind of gift is this, my friend? Twenty middle-of-nowhere towns!" And people still call them that today. That's all Hiram got from Solomon for over four and a half tons of gold!

Here's the rundown of the labor force King Solomon put together to build God's Temple, his palace, the Millo (a defensive structure), the wall of Jerusalem, and the fortified cities of Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.

The Pharaoh of Egypt had previously attacked and captured Gezer, burned it down, and killed all the Canaanites living there. He gave it as a wedding gift to his daughter, who was Solomon's wife. So, Solomon rebuilt Gezer.

He also built Lower Beth Horon, Baalath, and Tamar in the desert, along with storehouse towns in the countryside and towns for his chariots and horses. Solomon built a ton of stuff everywhere—in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and wherever else he felt like it.

Solomon rounded up all the people who weren't Israelites but were still living in the land (the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites) and forced them into slave labor, a practice that was still going on. But he didn't treat the actual Israelites this way. They served in his army and government, as leaders and commanders of his chariots and horsemen. They were also the 550 project managers in charge of the workforce for Solomon's building projects.
It was after Pharaoh's daughter moved up from the City of David to the palace Solomon built just for her that he built the Millo.

Three times a year, Solomon would worship at God's Altar, offering sacrifices and burning incense in God's presence. He was super generous and thorough with everything related to the Temple; he didn't cut any corners.

And get this—ships! King Solomon also built a fleet of ships at Ezion Geber, near Elath in Edom on the Red Sea. Hiram sent his experienced sailors to help Solomon's men. They sailed to Ophir, brought back sixteen tons of gold, and gave it all to King Solomon.

title: Queen of Sheba Tests Solomon's Wisdom (Spoiler: He's GOATED)
paragraphs: The queen of Sheba heard about Solomon and how he was tight with God. She showed up to see if he was all that, hitting him with some super hard questions. She rolled into Jerusalem with a whole squad, camels loaded with spices, a crazy amount of gold, and all these precious gems. She got real with Solomon, telling him everything on her mind. And Solomon? He had an answer for everything. Nothing was too hard for him. When the queen of Sheba saw for herself how wise Solomon was, and checked out the palace he built, the food they were serving, all the important people working for him and the waiters looking so sharp, the fancy glasses, and the insane worship setup with all the offerings at God's Temple, she was totally blown away.

She told the king, 'Yo, it's all true! Everything I heard back home about you being so successful and wise, it's no joke. I wouldn't have believed it if I didn't see it with my own eyes. People weren't even exaggerating! You're way more wise and classy than I ever imagined. The people who work for you are so lucky, they get to be around you every day and hear all your smarts firsthand! And shoutout to your God, who's obviously a big fan of you and made you king. It's clear God loves Israel a lot, putting you in charge to keep things fair and build a nation that honors Him.'
Then she gave the king a casual four and a half tons of gold, plus a ton of spices and expensive gems. There's never been a spice delivery like the one the queen of Sheba brought to King Solomon.

Hiram's ships also brought in gold from Ophir, along with tons of fragrant sandalwood and pricey gems. The king used the sandalwood to make fancy cabinets for God's Temple and the palace, and also for harps and other instruments for the musicians. No one's seen sandalwood like that since.
King Solomon, in return, gave the queen of Sheba everything she wanted—whatever she asked for, on top of all the generous gifts he'd already given her. She was happy and went back home with her crew.
Solomon was raking in about twenty-five tons of gold every year. And that wasn't even counting the money from taxes and trade with merchants and all the other kings and governors.

King Solomon made two hundred huge shields out of hammered gold—each one had like seven and a half pounds of gold in it—and three hundred smaller shields that were about half that size. He kept them in a place called the House of the Forest of Lebanon.

The king also had this massive throne made of ivory with gold details. It had six steps leading up to it, and the back was curved. There were lions on both sides of the armrests. And there were twelve more lions, one at each end of the six steps. No other kingdom had a throne that cool.

All of King Solomon's cups and mugs were made of gold, and all the dishes and stuff in the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. Nothing was made of silver; silver was considered basic and cheap back then.
The king had a fleet of ships that sailed with Hiram's ships. Every three years, they'd come back with a haul of gold, silver, ivory, and even apes and peacocks.

King Solomon was wiser and richer than any other king on earth—he was just on another level. People came from all over the world to hang with Solomon and soak up the wisdom God gave him. And everyone who visited brought gifts—cool things made of gold and silver, stylish clothes, the newest weapons, exotic spices, and horses and mules. It was like a parade of visitors, year after year.

Solomon started collecting chariots and horses: fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horses! He kept them in special cities for chariots and also in Jerusalem. The king made silver so common it was like picking up rocks, and cedar wood was as common as the fig trees in the hills. His horses were imported from Egypt and Cilicia, bought by his own agents. Chariots from Egypt cost about fifteen pounds of silver, and a horse was about three and three-quarters pounds. Solomon was running a major horse-trading business with the Hittite and Aramean kings.

title: King Solomon's Epic Fail
paragraphs: King Solomon was obsessed with women. Pharaoh's daughter was only the first; he had a whole squad of foreign wives—Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women. These were the exact nations God had warned Israel about, saying, 'Don't you dare marry them, or they'll get you hooked on their sketchy gods.' But Solomon, being extra, fell hard for them and just couldn't let them go. He had 700 wives who were basically royalty and another 300 concubines. A thousand women! And yeah, they totally turned his heart away from God. As he got older, his wives played him, getting him into their foreign gods, and he wasn't loyal to his God anymore, not like his dad David had been. He started worshipping Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, and Molech, the super messed-up god of the Ammonites.

Solomon straight-up defied God; he didn't follow his dad David's example at all. He even built a whole shrine for Chemosh, the gross god of Moab, and for Molech, the Ammonites' nasty god, on a hill right next to Jerusalem. He did this for all his foreign wives, and soon the whole country was stinking of their weird sacrifices.

God was seriously ticked off at Solomon for ghosting the God of Israel, the same God who had shown up for him twice and told him straight up not to mess with other gods. Solomon completely ignored God's orders.

God told Solomon, 'Look, since this is how you're gonna be, breaking our deal and ignoring my commands, I'm ripping the kingdom away from you and giving it to someone else. But, out of respect for your dad David, I won't do it while you're still alive. Your son is gonna get the short end of the stick—I'll snatch it right from him. Even then, I won't take everything. I'll leave him one tribe, for my boy David's sake and for Jerusalem, the city I chose.'

So God stirred up trouble against Solomon through Hadad, a descendant of the king of Edom. Years earlier, when David devastated Edom, Joab, the commander of the army, went to bury the dead and massacred all the men of Edom. Joab and his army stayed there six months, making sure they'd killed every man in Edom. Hadad, just a boy at the time, escaped with some Edomites who had worked for his father. They escaped through Midian to Paran, picked up more men in Paran, and went on to Egypt, to Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Pharaoh gave Hadad a house, food, and land. Pharaoh liked him so much that he gave him his wife's sister, Queen Tahpenes, in marriage. She had a son named Genubath, who was raised like one of the royal family and grew up in the palace with Pharaoh's own kids.
While he was chilling in Egypt, Hadad heard that David and his general Joab were both dead. So he went to Pharaoh and said, 'Aight, I'm out. I wanna go back to my own country.'
Pharaoh was like, 'But why? You wanna leave? Is something wrong? Don't you like it here?'
Hadad said, 'Nah, it's all good, but for real, I gotta go home. Just let me dip.'

Then God raised up another hater for Solomon: Rezon, son of Eliada. This dude had bailed on his boss, King Hadadezer of Zobah. After David beat the Arameans, Rezon got a crew of rebels together and became their leader. They ended up in Damascus, and Rezon became king there. Just like Hadad, Rezon was a major pain for Israel during Solomon's entire reign. He ruled over Aram and straight-up hated Israel.
And then, the final straw: Jeroboam, son of Nebat, rebelled against the king. He was an Ephraimite from Zeredah, and his mom was a widow named Zeruah. He was actually one of Solomon's officials.

Here's why he rebelled. Solomon had built the outer defense system (the Millo) and had fixed the walls that had been crumbling since his dad David's time. Jeroboam stood out during the construction as strong and able. Solomon saw how good he was and put him in charge of all the workers from the tribe of Joseph.

One day, Jeroboam was walking out of Jerusalem when he bumped into the prophet Ahijah from Shiloh. Ahijah was rocking a brand-new cloak. It was just the two of them on this empty road. Ahijah dramatically took off his new cloak and ripped it into twelve pieces.

He told Jeroboam, 'Take ten of these. This is a message from the God of Israel: Listen—I'm ripping the kingdom from Solomon and giving you ten tribes. He gets to keep one, for my servant David's sake and for Jerusalem, the city I chose. And here's why: He ditched me and started worshipping Ashtoreth, goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh, god of the Moabites, and Molech, god of the Ammonites. He hasn't been living right, hasn't done what I wanted, and hasn't followed the rules like his dad David did.'

'But, I'm not gonna take the whole kingdom from him right now. I'll let him be king for his lifetime, because of my man David, who I chose and who actually followed my rules. But after Solomon's gone, I'll take the kingdom from his son and give you ten tribes. I'll leave his son one tribe, so there's always a light for my servant David in Jerusalem, the city I chose for my Name.'

'But you? I've chosen you. You're gonna be king of Israel, and you can rule however you want. If you listen to me, live the way I show you, do what's right, and follow my commands like David did, I'll have your back. I'll build you a dynasty as solid as David's. Israel is yours! I'm bringing the hurt to David's descendants, but it won't last forever.'
Solomon tried to have Jeroboam assassinated, but he dipped and escaped to Egypt. He got asylum with King Shishak and stayed there until Solomon died.

The rest of Solomon's story—his reign, his projects, his wisdom—you can read all about it in *The Chronicles of Solomon*. Solomon ruled all of Israel from Jerusalem for forty years. Then he died and was buried in the City of David, his father's city. His son Rehoboam took over as the next king.

title: The Kingdom Splits?! Rehoboam's EPIC Fail
paragraphs: Alright, so Rehoboam heads over to Shechem, 'cause all of Israel was there to make him the new king. Meanwhile, this guy Jeroboam, who had been hiding out in Egypt to get away from King Solomon, heard Solomon was dead and came back home.

Rehoboam gets Jeroboam and all the people together. They hit him with this: "Yo, your dad made life crazy hard for us—like, he worked us to the bone. Give us a break, lighten up a little, and we'll be your loyal crew."
Rehoboam's like, "Give me three days to think about it, then come back."
So, King Rehoboam chats with the elders, the old guys who advised his dad. He's like, "What's your advice? What should I tell these people?"
They said, "If you just serve the people, listen to what they need, and be cool with them, they'll literally do anything for you."

But nah, he blew off the elders' advice and went to his boys, the young guys he grew up with who were just trying to get on his good side. "What do you guys think? What should I say to these people complaining about my dad being too harsh?"

His crew, the young hotheads, were like, "These people complaining? Tell 'em this: 'My pinky finger is thicker than my dad's whole waist. You think my dad was tough? You haven't seen anything yet. My dad hit you with whips; I'm gonna come at you with scorpion whips!'" It was a terrible idea.

Three days later, Jeroboam and the people came back, just like Rehoboam said. And the king's answer was super harsh and rude. He totally ignored the elders and went with his friends' advice: "You thought my dad was tough? You ain't seen nothing. My dad used whips; I'm using scorpion whips!"
Rehoboam just wouldn't listen to the people. But this was all part of God's plan, to make good on the promise He made to Jeroboam son of Nebat through Ahijah the prophet.

When all of Israel saw the king wasn't listening to them at all, they basically said, "Forget you, David's family! We're done with you! Let's bounce, Israel! From now on, David's house can take care of itself."
And just like that, they left. But Rehoboam was still king over the people living in the towns of Judah.

Later, when King Rehoboam sent out Adoniram, the guy in charge of the labor force, the Israelites ganged up on him, threw stones at him, and killed him. King Rehoboam had to jump in his chariot and escape to Jerusalem ASAP. And Israel has been rebelling against the Davidic dynasty ever since.
When the news got out that Jeroboam was back, the people invited him and made him king over all of Israel. The only tribe left for the Davidic dynasty was Judah.
When Rehoboam got back to Jerusalem, he gathered 180,000 of his best soldiers from Judah and Benjamin to go fight Israel and take back his kingdom.

But then, God spoke to a man of God named Shemaiah: "Tell Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and everyone in Judah and Benjamin, and anyone else who's around: God says, 'Don't go fight your own relatives, the Israelites. Everyone go home. I'm in control here.'" And they actually listened. They did what God said and went home.
Jeroboam built up the city of Shechem in the hills of Ephraim and made it his capital. He also fortified a place called Penuel.

But then Jeroboam started thinking, "It's only a matter of time before the kingdom goes back to David's side. As soon as these people start going back to the Temple of God in Jerusalem to worship, they'll start wanting Rehoboam as their king again. Then they'll kill me and go back to him."

So the king came up with a new plan: He made two golden calves. Then he announced, "It's way too much of a hassle to go all the way to Jerusalem to worship. Look! Here are the gods who brought you out of Egypt!" He put one calf in a city called Bethel and the other in Dan. This was a huge sin. Like, for real, people started traveling all the way to Dan just to worship a golden calf!

And it didn't stop there. Jeroboam built a bunch of unauthorized shrines all over and made priests out of anyone he could find, whether they were qualified or not. To top it all off, he made up his own holy New Year holiday on the fifteenth day of the eighth month to compete with the festival in Judah. He even led the worship himself at the altar in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves he had made. He staffed Bethel with priests from the local shrines he had made. This whole thing was his own idea, a festival just for Israel, with him at the center of it all.

title: Prophet Gets Played, Pays the Ultimate Price
paragraphs: So check this out. King Jeroboam was at the altar in Bethel, about to make an offering, when a man of God from Judah shows up, sent by God himself. He walks right up to the altar and calls it out, saying, 'Altar, Altar! This is a message from God: A son named Josiah will be born into David's family. He's going to sacrifice the priests of these high places who are making offerings on you—right on you! They're gonna burn human bones on you!' And to prove it, he said, 'Here's the sign God is giving: This altar will split apart, and the offerings on it will spill into the dirt.'

When the king heard the message the man of God preached against the altar at Bethel, he reached out to grab him, yelling, 'Arrest that guy!' But instantly, the arm he reached out with was paralyzed, just hanging there, totally useless. And at that exact moment, the altar split apart and the offerings spilled out, just like the man of God had said would happen as a sign from God.
The king, totally freaked out, begged the man of God, 'Please, pray to your God for me! Ask him to heal my arm!' So the man of God prayed, and the king's arm was healed, good as new.
Then the king said to the man of God, 'Hey, come home with me for a meal. I want to give you a gift.'

But the man of God told the king, 'No way. Even if you offered me half of your entire palace, I wouldn't go with you. I won't eat or drink anything in this place. God gave me strict orders: ‘Don’t eat any food, don’t drink any water, and don’t go back the same way you came.’' So he left, taking a different road from the one he had used to get to Bethel.
Now, there was this old prophet living in Bethel. His sons came and told him everything the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They told their dad everything he had said to the king.
Their father asked, 'Which way did he go?' His sons showed him the road the man of God from Judah had taken.
He told his sons, 'Saddle my donkey for me.' So they saddled the donkey, he got on, and rode off after the man of God. He found him sitting under an oak tree.
He asked him, 'Are you the man of God who came from Judah?'
'Yeah, that's me,' he replied.
'Well, come home with me and have something to eat.'

'Sorry, can't do it,' the man of God said. 'I can't go back with you, and I can't eat or drink with you here. I'm under strict orders from God: ‘Don’t eat any food, don’t drink any water, and don’t go back the same way you came.’'

But the old prophet said, 'Hey, I'm a prophet too, just like you. And an angel came to me with a message from God: ‘Bring him back to your house so he can eat and drink.’' But he was totally lying. So the man of God went back with him and ate and drank in his house.

While they were sitting at the table, a message from God came to the old prophet who had brought him back. He yelled at the man of God from Judah, 'This is God's word to you: You have defied God's command and didn't obey the order your God gave you. You came back and ate and drank in the place where he told you not to. Because of that, you'll die far from home, and your body won't be buried in your family's tomb.'

After they finished eating, the old prophet saddled the donkey for the man of God he had brought back. As he was riding away, a lion found him on the road and killed him. His body was just lying there on the road, with the donkey standing on one side and the lion on the other. Some people walking by saw the body on the road and the lion standing next to it. They went into the town where the old prophet lived and told everyone what they saw.

When the prophet who had tricked him heard the news, he said, 'It's the man of God who disobeyed God's direct order. God handed him over to the lion, which mauled and killed him, just like God said it would.'

The prophet told his sons, 'Saddle my donkey.' They did, and he went and found the body lying in the road, with the donkey and the lion still standing there. The lion hadn't eaten the body or attacked the donkey. The prophet put the man of God's body on his donkey and brought it back to his town to mourn and bury him. He laid the body in his own tomb, and they all cried, 'Oh, my brother, how tragic!'

After the burial, the prophet said to his sons, 'When I die, bury me in the same tomb where the man of God is buried. Lay my bones next to his. Because the message he preached from God against the altar in Bethel and all the other shrines in Samaria will for sure happen.'

Even after all this, Jeroboam didn't change his evil ways. He kept recruiting priests for the forbidden shrines without any standards—anyone who wanted to be a priest at one of the local shrines could be one. This was the huge sin of Jeroboam's kingdom, and it's what ultimately led to its downfall and destruction.

title: The Queen's Disguise & A Doomed Kingdom
paragraphs: So, around this time, Jeroboam's son Abijah got super sick. Jeroboam told his wife, "Quick, go in disguise. Put on a disguise so nobody knows you're the queen and head over to Shiloh. The prophet Ahijah lives there—yeah, the same guy who said I'd be king. Take him ten loaves of bread, some sweet pastries, and a jar of honey. Go see him, and he'll tell us what's up with our son."

Jeroboam's wife did exactly that. She went straight to Shiloh, to Ahijah's house. Ahijah was really old by then and couldn't see a thing, but God had given him a heads-up: "Jeroboam's wife is coming to ask about her sick son; here's what you tell her."

When she walked in, all disguised, Ahijah heard her and said, "Come on in, wife of Jeroboam! Why the whole fakeout? I've got some seriously bad news for you. Go tell Jeroboam this message I got straight from God, the God of Israel: 'I pulled you out of nowhere and made you the leader of my people. I snatched the kingdom from David's family and handed it to you. But you were nothing like my servant David, who actually listened to me and was all in for me. Instead, you've been wild, setting a new record for evil by making fake gods—literal tin gods! You've pushed me away and turned your back on me, and I'm so done.'

"And I'm not gonna stand for it. I'm bringing disaster on your whole family, Jeroboam. I'm wiping out every single male, whether they're a slave or free. Your family has become trash, and I'm taking it out. Any of your family who die in the city will be eaten by stray dogs, and any who die in the countryside will be eaten by vultures. That's a promise from God.

"So, that's the deal. Go home. The second you get back to town, the boy will die. Everyone will come to his funeral and be super sad. He's the only one in Jeroboam's whole family who will get a proper burial because he's the only one God has anything good to say about.

"Then God's gonna set up a new king over Israel who will completely destroy your family, like, wipe them off the face of the earth. It's doomsday for you, Jeroboam! God's gonna shake up Israel like a storm, pull them up by the roots from this good land he gave them, and scatter them to the four winds. Why? Because you all made God so mad with your gross Asherah sex-and-religion shrines. He's just gonna give up on Israel because of your sins, Jeroboam, which you led everyone else into."

Jeroboam's wife left and went back home to Tirzah. The moment she walked through the door, the boy died. They buried him, and everyone was heartbroken, just like God had said through his prophet Ahijah.

The rest of Jeroboam's story, all the wars he fought and how he ruled, is all written down in the official records of the kings of Israel. He was king for 22 years, then he died and was buried with his ancestors. His son Nadab took over as king.

Meanwhile, Rehoboam, Solomon's son, was king in Judah. He was 41 when he started and ruled for 17 years in Jerusalem, the city God chose out of all the tribes for his Name to be worshipped. Rehoboam's mom was Naamah, an Ammonite. The people of Judah were being openly wicked, which made God furious. They were even worse than their ancestors, setting new records for sin. They built these nasty Asherah sex-and-religion shrines and sacred stones all over the place—on hills, under trees, you name it. Even worse, they had male prostitutes at the shrines, making the whole country disgusting—it was all the stuff God had cleared out when he brought Israel into the land in the first place.

In the fifth year of King Rehoboam's rule, King Shishak of Egypt attacked Jerusalem. He totally looted the Temple of God and the royal palace, taking all the treasure. He cleaned them out, even taking the gold shields Solomon had made. King Rehoboam had to replace them with bronze shields and gave them to the palace guards. Whenever the king went to the Temple, the guards would carry the shields, but they always had to put them back in the guardroom afterward.

The rest of Rehoboam's life is all written down in the official records of the kings of Judah. There was non-stop war between him and Jeroboam. Rehoboam died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His mom was Naamah, an Ammonite. His son Abijah became the next king.

title: Royal Rumble: Judah's Messy King Drama
paragraphs: So, in the 18th year of the rule of Jeroboam son of Nebat, this guy Abijah became the new king of Judah. He only ruled for three years in Jerusalem. His mom was Maacah, who was Absalom's daughter. And honestly, he was a carbon copy of his dad, making the same mistakes and messing up. His heart wasn't fully in it with God, not like his great-grandpa David. But even with all that, God showed him some grace for David's sake and kept the family line going with a son to follow him, keeping Jerusalem safe. Because David, for real, lived a life that honored God, almost always following God's directions (except for that one time with Uriah the Hittite). But yeah, the beef between Abijah and Jeroboam was nonstop the whole time.

The rest of Abijah's story, everything he did, is all written down in the history books of Judah's kings. But that war with Jeroboam was the main event of his life. Then Abijah died and was buried with his family in Jerusalem. His son Asa became the next king.
In the 20th year of King Jeroboam's rule in Israel, Asa started his reign over Judah. He was king in Jerusalem for 41 years. His grandma's name was Maacah.

Asa was a real one. He actually tried to follow God and live right, bringing back the good vibes of his ancestor David. He went on a major cleanup spree: he kicked out the temple prostitutes and tossed all the fake god statues his ancestors had collected. Asa didn't hold back; he even had to fire his own grandma, Queen Maacah, from her royal position because she'd set up this super gross and disrespectful statue for a fake goddess named Asherah. Asa literally wrecked it and burned the whole thing down in the Kidron Valley. He didn't manage to get rid of all the sketchy local shrines where people were mixing worship with other wild stuff, but his intentions were good—his heart was genuinely trying to be loyal to God. He took all the gold and silver stuff that he and his dad had dedicated to God and put it back in the Temple.

But for a big chunk of his reign, there was this ongoing war between him and King Baasha of Israel. Baasha started it. He built a fort at a place called Ramah to basically block the border, so nobody could get in or out of Judah.

So Asa took all the silver and gold left in God's Temple and his own palace, gave it to his officials, and sent them to Ben-Hadad son of Tabrimmon, son of Hezion, the king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus. The message was basically, "Yo, let's be allies, just like our dads were. Here's a gift of silver and gold to show I'm serious. Ditch your alliance with King Baasha of Israel so he'll back off and leave me alone."

Ben-Hadad agreed with King Asa. He took the deal and sent his army to attack the towns in Israel. He hit Ijon, Dan, Abel Beth Maacah, and the whole Kinnereth area, including Naphtali. When Baasha heard the news, he had to stop building his fort at Ramah and retreat to Tirzah.

Then King Asa made a new rule for everyone in Judah—no exceptions. They all had to go and carry away the timber and stones that Baasha had been using to build the fort at Ramah. Asa used all those materials to build up his own defenses at Geba and Mizpah.

The full story of Asa's life, all the cool stuff he did and the cities he fortified, is written in the history books of the kings of Judah. When he got old, he got a bad case of gout in his feet. Then Asa died and was buried with his ancestors in Jerusalem. His son Jehoshaphat took over as the next king.

Nadab, Jeroboam's son, became king of Israel during the second year of Asa's rule in Judah. He was king for two years, and he was straight-up bad news in God's eyes. He just followed his dad's terrible example, who not only sinned but dragged all of Israel down with him.

Then this guy Baasha son of Ahijah, from the tribe of Issachar, plotted against Nadab. He attacked and killed him while Nadab and the Israelite army were fighting the Philistines at Gibbethon. So, in the third year of King Asa's rule in Judah, Baasha killed Nadab and made himself the new king of Israel.

The first thing Baasha did as king was kill every single person in Jeroboam's family. Like, he left no one alive. He completely wiped them out, which is exactly what God's prophet Ahijah had said would happen. It was the payback for all of Jeroboam's sins and for how he made Israel sin, making the God of Israel furious.
The rest of Nadab's story is written in the history books of the kings of Israel. And that war between Asa and Baasha? It just kept going.

In the third year of King Asa's rule in Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became the king over all Israel in the city of Tirzah. He ruled for twenty-four years. And just like the others, he was openly evil in God's sight, following the exact same path as Jeroboam, who sinned and made Israel sin.

title: Israel's Kings: A Total Disaster
paragraphs: God's word came to this guy Jehu, son of Hanani, with a message for King Baasha. It was basically like, "Yo, I picked you up from nothing—you were a total nobody—and made you the leader of my people, Israel. But what did you do? You just kept doing the same dumb stuff as Jeroboam, leading my people to sin and making me seriously angry. So now, get ready for the consequences. I'm about to completely destroy you and your entire family, the same way I got rid of Jeroboam son of Nebat. Any of your people who die in the city will get eaten by stray dogs, and the ones who die out in the country will be food for the crows."
The rest of Baasha's story, everything he did as king, is written down in the official records of Israel's kings. Baasha died and was buried in Tirzah, and his son Elah took over as king.

So yeah, that's what happened with Baasha. God's message came to him and his family through the prophet Jehu son of Hanani because he was so openly evil in God's eyes and made God so mad. He was just like Jeroboam, even though God had already taken Jeroboam out.

In the 26th year that Asa was king of Judah, Elah, Baasha's son, started his rule. He was king in Tirzah for only two years. One day, he was at the house of Arza, the guy who managed the palace, just getting wasted. That's when Zimri, who was the captain of half his chariots, plotted against him. Zimri snuck in, knocked Elah out, and killed him. This all went down in the 27th year of King Asa's reign in Judah. And just like that, Zimri became the new king.

The second Zimri was king, he went and killed everyone connected to Baasha's family. He got rid of all of them—relatives, friends, everyone. Zimri totally wiped out Baasha's entire family, exactly like God had said would happen through the prophet Jehu. It was payback for the sins of Baasha and his son Elah, not just for their own sins, but for dragging all of Israel into it and making the God of Israel angry with their pointless idols.
The rest of Elah's life, everything he did and said, is written in the official records of Israel's kings.

So Zimri was king in Tirzah for a grand total of seven days. This was during the 27th year Asa was king of Judah. At the time, the Israelite army was camped out near a Philistine town called Gibbethon. When the army heard the news, "Zimri has betrayed and killed the king," they made their commander, Omri, the new king right then and there. Omri and the whole army immediately left Gibbethon and went to attack Tirzah. When Zimri saw the city was surrounded and he was basically a dead man, he went into the strongest part of the palace, set the whole place on fire, and died in it. It was a fitting end for all his sins, for living such an evil life in God's eyes, following in Jeroboam's footsteps, sinning, and then dragging Israel down with him.
As for the rest of Zimri's story, including his wild conspiracy, it's all written down in the official records of Israel's kings.

After that, the people of Israel were split. Half of them wanted this guy Tibni, son of Ginath, to be king, and the other half wanted Omri. In the end, Omri's side was stronger than Tibni's. Tibni ended up dead, and Omri became the king.

Omri became king of Israel in the 31st year of King Asa's reign in Judah. He ruled for twelve years, with the first six in Tirzah. Then he bought a hill called Samaria from a guy named Shemer for 150 pounds of silver. He built up the hill and named the city he built there Samaria, after the original owner, Shemer.
